doc.title: JJ Johnson — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Charles Mingus
summary: Johnson met Mingus in that period, recorded once on a trombone workshop album, and remembers him as a maverick.

story.theme_name: Leading a band: choosing, paying and managing players

blocks.x: Was this also the time when you first met Charles Mingus, or does that come at a later time?

More than likely it was during that cycle that I first met Charles Mingus. I don’t remember the circumstances or the incident in which I met Charles Mingus, but I did meet him at some point. I never worked a lot with Charles Mingus. I don’t know that
I ever recorded with Mingus. Did I?
Yes. You did. The one time. It was the trombone workshop album.
[Reissued on CD as Four Trombones: The Debut Recordings.]
Trombone Workshop. Oh, yes, yes, you’re right. Yeah. But that wasn’t Mingus’s band, was it?
No, it was an all-star band.
That comes back to me, now that you mention it.
Would you like to comment at all about Charles Mingus and your activity with him, your relationship with him, your impressions of Charles Mingus?

My first impression of Charles Mingus, as I recall it, was the impression that remained with me throughout my friendship and exposure to Charles Mingus, in that it was that Charles Mingus marched to the beat of his own drum and to the beat of no other drum. He was a maverick in the classic sense of the word. He did not speak with forked tongue. He was oftentimes categorized as being controversial. He was even characterized in some factions as being a troublemaker. He was a guy who had strong opinions, for example, about the racial situation in this country and the racial situation in the world. He injected some of this opinionated feeling about that matter in some of his compositions, with lyrics to some of his compositions that made commentaries about the racial situation in the world and what not.
Yeah. I loved his title that I can’t even pronounce – Pithecanthropus Erectus.
